idiom_name: Stream with lazy intermediate operations and Stream.iterate/generate
implementation_notes: Java's lazy collection is the Stream: the package documentation calls filtering, mapping and duplicate removal laziness-seeking because nothing runs until a terminal operation executes, and Stream.iterate/generate produce unbounded sources that takeWhile/limit bound - a stream is a one-shot view over its source, not a data structure. Because a stream cannot be reused and is not memoized, the alternatives are collecting it deliberately (List/Iterator) or writing an Iterable with a caching step; keep a plain collection when the data is small or traversed repeatedly.
code_sketch:
Stream.iterate(new BigInteger[]{BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ONE},
                p -> new BigInteger[]{p[1], p[0].add(p[1])})
      .map(p -> p[0])
      .filter(n -> n.testBit(0))       // nothing has run yet
      .limit(10)                       // bound the infinite source
      .forEach(System.out::println);   // terminal operation forces elements
pitfalls: A stream is consumed at most once: a second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException (or 'stream has already been operated upon or closed'), so it cannot be stored as if it were a collection.
A stream over a lazily opened resource (Files.lines, try-with-resources) must be closed in try-with-resources; forgetting it leaks the file handle even though the stream looks lazy and harmless.
Intermediate operations are deferred, so exceptions arrive at the terminal call, and an unbounded source without limit/takeWhile hangs there.

variants.name: Custom Iterable/Iterator with a memoizing cell
variants.idiom_name: Iterable<T> returning a fresh Iterator backed by a cached supplier
variants.implementation_notes: When the sequence must be re-iterable, thread-safe or inspectable, Java's answer is a hand-written Iterable whose iterator materialises elements into an internal cache on first access (a Supplier plus a memo cell per element), so the lazy work happens once and later traversals read the cache; unlike a stream it can be passed around like a collection and iterated again. The classic form is justified exactly here - streams cannot express it - and pays for it with memory proportional to the realized prefix and with concurrency work if several threads force the same element.
pitfalls: Memoizing lazily without a bound retains every realized element for the lifetime of the list object (the lazy-list space leak); provide a drop/clear policy for long-lived sequences.
Sharing one lazily computing Iterable across threads needs synchronization or a thread-safe cache, otherwise two threads compute the same element twice or see a partially built list.
Iterator contract bugs (hasNext consuming an element, next without hasNext, NoSuchElementException timing) are easy to introduce in hand-written lazy iterators and hard to test.
